blocks.text: JOACHIM ROMAIN — LOOKING AT WHAT OTHERS NO LONGER SEE

Joachim Romain looks at images precisely where they generally cease to interest us. Torn posters, amputated letters, anonymous faces, faded urban signs, visual debris: His domain is not that of the spectacular image, but that of what remains after it. Since his early days in street photography, he has extracted fragments from the urban environment that the ordinary gaze has learned to overlook, removing them from their status as waste and giving them another existence. For Romain, to photograph is already to displace. This gesture lies at the heart of a practice that has never fully accepted the boundaries between photography, urban art, collage, and installation. He does not regard these mediums as separate territories, but as different states of the same gaze. Photography captures, appropriation isolates, collage recomposes, and installation displaces once again. What interests him, then, is less the image itself than what it becomes when its context changes when it loses its original function and acquires a new visual charge. An advertising poster is no longer simply a poster once it has been torn; a fragment of a letter is no longer merely a sign once it becomes material; a face torn from an image can suddenly become the portrait of an era. There is a form of contemporary archaeology at work here. But it is an archaeology without nostalgia. Romain does not seek to preserve the traces of the city; he puts them into tension. He is interested in the way images appear, disappear, overlap, and ultimately generate a memory of their own. His work reveals a city that is constantly producing and destroying its own representations. Through it, he also questions our relationship to images: their omnipresence, their speed of circulation, their obsolescence, and their strange ability, despite their proliferation, to become invisible. His gaze naturally belongs to a history of urban art in which Jacques Villeglé stands as one of its defining figures. Yet with Romain, the lineage is never simply a matter of quotation. Where Villeglé turned the wall into a space of revelation, collecting the anonymous tears of public posters as signs of a collective memory, Romain works within a landscape saturated with images, where the fragment no longer comes from the street alone. It also comes from the digital realm, commerce, advertising, screens, and a new visual economy in which everything is produced, consumed, and replaced almost instantaneously.

His participation in the exhibition devoted to Jacques Villeglé at the Musée Carnavalet takes on a particular resonance in this context. It places his work within a history that continually reinvents itself: that of artists who do not necessarily create their images from nothing but know how to recognize an image that is already there, buried beneath another, and give it a second life. For Romain, this act of revelation operates as much through photography as through material, gesture, and composition. It is precisely this logic of displacement that emerges in Défragmentation at Galerie Laurent Rigail. Alongside Jacques Villeglé, Quentin DMR, and the other artists brought together for the exhibition, Romain contributes to a reflection on the fragment as artistic material: a fragment of the city, of memory, of a poster, a photograph, or a sign. Yet the exhibition’s title could almost describe his own method. To defragment is not simply to break an image into pieces. It is to alter the relationships between those pieces in order to make something else appear. This idea runs throughout his work. Even when he photographs, Romain does not simply record. He selects. He frames. He excludes. Through the choice of what he decides to look at, he is already transforming reality. “Framing one part often makes you forget the rest,” he says in this questionnaire. The phrase could serve as a key to his entire practice. Because this is precisely where his art begins: in the awareness that looking is always an act of selection and that a fragment can sometimes say more than a complete image. His relationship to photography is therefore less documentary than critical. What matters is not only what the image shows, but what it leaves outside the frame, what it conceals, and what it suddenly allows us to see. Hence his recurring attention to detail, accident, and to that which is “not there for everyone else.” Romain searches for cracks in the surface of things. He finds stories there, tensions, sometimes simply an emotion. His visual practice extends this investigation without resolving it. He transforms visual waste into material but refuses to strip it of its disorder. He does not clean up the fragment; he allows it to retain the traces of its passage. Perhaps this is where the singularity of his gaze lies. In a world where images have become instantly available, retouched, and reproducible, Romain continues to search for those that have lived for images that still bear the marks of their own disappearance.

To look at the world with Joachim Romain is therefore to accept slowing down before what we have learned to pass without seeing. A worn letter. A half-erased face. A torn poster. A fragment of the city. Nothing, apparently. And yet, within that almost nothing, the possibility of an image.

Actu : Exhibitions : « Défragmentation » from oct 14th to nov. 14th 2026 Galerie Laurent Rigail 40, rue Volta 75003 Paris
Participation to the exhibition « Paris à l’arraché » dedicated to Jacques Villeglé at Musée Carnavalet.
What was your first photographic trigger? Joachim Romain: My father was a photographer. For my 15th birthday, he gave me a Nikon EM.
A photographic memory from your childhood? Joachim Romain: Me on the beach, photographed by my father.
The camera of your childhood? Joachim Romain: Polaroid, of course.
The one you use today? Joachim Romain: Canon 6D.
The man or woman of the image who inspired you? Joachim Romain: Brassaï.
The image you wish you had taken? Joachim Romain: The Woodstock album cover. I would have done two crazy things.
The one that moved you the most? Joachim Romain: Lee Friedlander.
And the one that made you angry? Joachim Romain: Marine mammals caught in fishing nets.
Which photograph changed the world? Joachim Romain: “Tank Man,” in Tiananmen Square.

And which photograph changed your world? Joachim Romain: A worn-out letter B and a face on a poster, photographed in Sarajevo in 2006. That image profoundly changed my photographic work and the subjects I research today.
What interests you most in an image? Joachim Romain: Its emotion.
What details do you look for in a face, a landscape, or an object? Joachim Romain: The one that isn’t there for everyone else.
Elliott Erwitt once said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? Joachim Romain: To some extent, yes. But why choose?

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? Joachim Romain: For me, technique comes after the subject and the framing. But it remains a very important part, depending on the effect you want to achieve with your subject.
Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? Joachim Romain: Absolutely not.
What can make silence visible in a photograph? Joachim Romain: A detail.
Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Joachim Romain: The moment is unique and that’s everything.
Can a photograph be more truthful than reality? Joachim Romain: That’s where staging comes into play.
Can a photograph change our perception of an event? Joachim Romain: Clearly. Focusing on one part often makes you forget the rest.
Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? Joachim Romain: For me, a testimony above all.
What makes a good photograph? Joachim Romain: The emotion it gives you.
What quality is essential to being a good photographer? Joachim Romain: Going out to find your subject and waiting for the right moment.

How do you choose your projects? Joachim Romain: They are connected to my visual art practice, although originally it was the other way around: my street photography gradually gave birth to my visual art practice. Today, the two have become one body of work in which photography and visual art come together.

How would you describe your creative process? Joachim Romain: It depends on the work. With the photographic series Fast_Shop , for example, there is a whole research process beforehand, followed by a real exploration of movement and time.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? Joachim Romain: My project Made in Europe is about creating an exhibition that brings my street work, photography, and installation into dialogue.
The person you would like to photograph? Joachim Romain: my daughter, and I did it! But I’d happily do it again.
The person you would like to be photographed by? Joachim Romain: Mari Katayama or Zanele Muholi.
One essential photography book? Joachim Romain: Affichage_Libre 🙂 Otherwise, Chernobyl by Robert Polidori. And a book by Brassaï, Brassaï: Picasso and the Photographs , or Vivian Maier.
What is the last photograph you took? Joachim Romain: Portraits of artists in Turkey, in Izmir.
On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok — and why? Joachim Romain: Instagram. There hasn’t been anything fun on Facebook for a while. And I’m not on TikTok at all.
What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? Joachim Romain: The quality, the framing… A bit like when digital photography arrived and everyone thought they were a photographer.
One Instagram account everyone should follow? Joachim Romain: Your friends’. The rest isn’t important.

What is your view on AI? Joachim Romain: A bit like when the first Adobe Illustrator came along: it’s a development that is difficult to avoid, but one we need to learn to master. The most important thing, in my view, is to remain the creative force, rather than simply following or letting AI do the creating for us. But, in reality, I think we won’t be in control of much for very long.
Color or black and white? Joachim Romain: Both, but with a preference for black and white.
Natural or artificial light? Joachim Romain: Natural.
Which city strikes you as the most photogenic? Joachim Romain: Marseille.
The city, country, or culture you dream of discovering? Joachim Romain: Africa.
The place you never get tired of? Joachim Romain: My bathroom 🙂 Seriously, though, definitely the Arles festival.
The image that, for you, represents the state of the world today? Joachim Romain: The photomontage of British Prime Minister Tony Blair taking a selfie against a backdrop of burning oil.
What do you think is missing from the world today? Joachim Romain: A strong movement toward nature and living together. It’s frightening right now.
If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you go for a selfie with him? Joachim Romain: That’s too disconnected from reality for me, so…
Your favorite drug? Joachim Romain: My studio.
Your best way to switch off? Joachim Romain: I haven’t found one. I dream of it.
Your latest act of madness? Joachim Romain: A Get 27–Ricard cocktail in Arles 🙂 I still have a headache.
The body of work you are particularly proud of? Joachim Romain: My Urban work, which consists of transforming what everyone considers visual waste into an art installation.
The job you would never have wanted to do? Joachim Romain: I respect people so much that saying “I wouldn’t want to do your job” feels a bit harsh 🙂
Which question throws you off the most? Joachim Romain: Who is your favorite artist?
The last thing you did for the first time? Joachim Romain: Rowing on the Olympic rowing basin in Montreal, with my family. It was great.
Your biggest regret? Joachim Romain: Not having gone to art school.
If you could start all over again? Joachim Romain: Maybe I would have taken school more seriously. But then again, I wouldn’t have had the path I’ve had, and I don’t regret it.
If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table? Joachim Romain: Jim Morrison, Nina Kraviz, Jacques Villeglé, Anselm Kiefer. Music and art: everything I love.
What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? Joachim Romain: If they remember me at all, that’s already something 🙂
The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? Joachim Romain: Generous.
One last word? Joachim Romain: Together.
